review_text_raw: I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

review_text_raw:
I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

review_text_raw:
I would prefer to give this game a 5/10, but unfortunately, that's not possible on Steam, so I’m rating it negatively for interested buyers to see.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

review_text_raw:
I absolutely love this game’s design and idea but sadly I don't think it was executed very well.

Rather than feeling in control of the narrative, most of the game was spent watching the story unfold with little player-contribution. There were different options to choose during conversations, which would somewhat influence the story plot-wise, but given that it's a mystery game and the choice of options available were very limited and surface-level (e.g. will you lie or not lie), replaying it to see what else (if anything) could have happened doesn't feel worth my time.

The story had some small unexpected and exciting twists, however most of these developments were overshadowed by the main plot being very predictable. I think if they had delved more into the individual cases within the game itself and focused less on forming an overarching plot, it would have been much more enjoyable.

The nature of the game put it in a great position to deliver really varied and unique puzzles (e.g. code breaking, crime solving, hacking -- all of which were very fun), yet the quantity of puzzles was seriously lacking. It felt like maybe only an hour out of the 3.5 hours of time spent playing was actually focused on problem-solving and the rest was in tedious over-explanatory conversation. 

I understand this is tagged with visual novel and so maybe the developers intended it for it to be more of a narrative-based experience, but if that is the reason for the lack of puzzles, I would have expected the plot to be more developed and have less of an obvious ending.

review_text_raw:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

The game has a great concept and some thrilling moments. The developers did a fantastic job immersing you in the feeling of being a "cog in a machine". The music, interface design, story theme, and execution were excellent. I especially enjoyed the quiet moments where I could read through various documents and explore the backstory and world the developers created.

That’s why it pains me so much that all this hard work feels utterly underutilized. You’re essentially handheld and dragged through a linear story, with little to no impact from your choices. There are intricate mechanics that seem fun once you struggle through their first use, but they are never used again. It is just a little bit more "game" than a "interactive movie".

I don’t want to be cruel—I can see the developers put a lot of effort into it—but it was just far too short.

I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

I think the game and the developer have a lot of potential and I believe that if the second game fixes all these issues, it can be GREAT.

This is going to be the oddest negative review I have ever left. This game got me philosophical about reviews: Is a game review to describe whether I think the game is well made? Or is the game review to describe whether I enjoyed it? It's so rare that these two things are out of alignment, I wasn't sure what to write here. I have decided to write a review based on my enjoyment.

So let me just say: This game is well made. It is VERY well made. It's mechanics are a little bit "Papers, Please", a little bit "Clandestine", and a little bit "The Roottrees are Dead" - all meant as a compliment. The production values are top notch. And the story is very well written and very engaging.

And that's where the problem comes in. When a game is this good, my enjoyment hinges on the story being satisfying - and this story is FAR from satisfying. The ending is a cliffhanger that should have been the INTRODUCTION to a game, not a game in itself. And aside from being an incomplete story, the ending is nothing but [spoiler]bad things happening to good people and bad people getting away with it[/spoiler]. And I find that an extremely unsatisfying experience.

So I leave this review to convey an experience for people like me: people who can appreciate a masterfully crafted game that delivers a deeply unsatisfying story. If I'd known how the story ended, I wouldn't have bothered.

review_text_raw:
EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.)
Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.")
I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless.
Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game. I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative. My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened. ORIGINAL REVIEW: Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game. First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once. The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content. I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again. **SPOILERS FOR THE END** The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.) Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.") I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless. Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

review_text_raw:
I had fun. I also almost requested a refund after finishing it because the ending made me so angry. [spoiler]It's not a happy ending, which is fine, but it's also not a satisfying ending. Choices are ultimately meaningless because an apparently superhuman hitman escapes custody in a high-security building (the story even makes a point of saying how secure this building is when you're helping another character find the passkey for the locker room) and is then apparently omniscient as he knows exactly where to find the director of this highly secure organization during a security lockdown, exactly when to intercept to main character en route to the exit, and is then able to ascend from the parking garage to the eighth floor to eliminate the supervisor/insider contact of our benevolent hacker companion all apparently without facing the slightest resistance from security in what is basically this universe's FBI HQ. Did the mole have him memorize the layout of the entire building? For what reason? After all that you're treated to a series of newspaper headlines letting you know that absolutely every ally you had over the course of the game is either dead, imprisoned, or missing. All tension goes out the window and it just turns into a cascade of tragedy for no clear reason. It's just so unbelievable to me. Maybe if it was clear from the start that this was more like a part 1 to a larger story or something, I would be more forgiving, but I expected a satisfying conclusion when I bought the game. Not super-hitman destroys everything because *dismissive raspberry sounds*[/spoiler]

With all that said, I do think the developer has a lot of potential. The puzzles were interesting and solving them felt really satisfying.

review_text_raw:
The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

Probably my mistake for expecting something akin to Hacknet from this game: it's FAR from that. 
The story is predictable and honestly feels like someone's first read of MKUltra on Wikipedia, interactivity with the computer & clues is [b]very[/b] limited (most introduced systems only get used literally once throughout the whole game) and it's just a very short game, which isn't fitting for its price tag. 
Other reviews mentioned that this game feels polished, but what's the point when it's so basic?.. Felt like I just wasted my time at the end of it, especially due to that sorry excuse of an ending.
